title: Observe unexpected methods on one read-only page
summary: Compare methods against a single endpoint contract. Keep the match expression separate from the action, and observe legitimate traffic before considering enforcement.

requires: A proxied hostname and an agreed method contract for the exact endpoint.
Enterprise entitlement for the custom-rule Log action used in this observation example.
excludes: Do not apply this GET/HEAD-only method set to write APIs, preflight endpoints, or an entire hostname.
This is not an authentication or authorization control.
dependencies: Existing terminating security rules can stop a request before this rule. Review rule order and the available analytics for your plan.

body.scope: Zone-level custom rule, www.example.com/public/about only. Replace this example hostname and endpoint with an owned, reviewed target.
conditions: Match the exact host and path.
Match methods outside the endpoint's agreed GET/HEAD set. Include OPTIONS if this endpoint needs CORS preflight.
availability: WAF custom rules exist on all plans with different quotas; the request-phase Log action requires Enterprise.
Where Log is unavailable, review available analytics before considering a narrowly scoped alternative. Do not substitute a browser challenge on an API.
body.expression: (http.host eq "www.example.com" and http.request.uri.path eq "/public/about" and not http.request.method in {"GET" "HEAD"})
body.action: Log for the observation phase; it does not block the matching request. Configure the action separately from the expression.
rollout: Inventory browser, health-check, integration, and CORS methods with the endpoint owner.
Validate the expression and configuration without treating a dry run as a real-traffic match test.
On an approved non-production hostname, enable Log and inspect representative legitimate requests. Decide separately whether enforcement is warranted.
validation: GET and HEAD should not match; an unexpected method on this exact path should match.
The same method on a different host or path should not match.
Verify required OPTIONS requests and account for rules that terminate evaluation earlier.
rollback: Disable this rule if scope or expected-method assumptions are wrong.
If later enforcement was approved, revert to observation or disable the rule, then confirm legitimate application behavior.

title: Browser access to a private origin with Access and Tunnel
summary: Publish a web application through a public hostname while keeping its origin off the public inbound path. Access makes the identity decision; Tunnel provides connectivity, not authorization.

requires: An HTTP(S) application reachable by cloudflared and an owned hostname routed through Cloudflare.
An Access self-hosted public application, identity provider, and a narrow application policy.
excludes: This public-hostname browser pattern is not private-IP routing, a site-to-site VPN, or general network access.
Non-browser clients need an explicitly chosen supported authentication flow; a login redirect is not an API credential.
dependencies: Confirm Access seat, logging, device-posture, and retention entitlements independently; this topology is not a universal plan promise.
Connector hosts need permitted outbound connectivity, DNS, and secure access to the origin. Protect connector credentials.

sources.title: Tunnel routing, replicas, and load balancing

assumptions: The user has a browser and the application supports an identity-aware reverse proxy.
The application is published at app.example.com. The hostname is public; the origin need not accept public inbound connections.
components: Browser, Cloudflare proxy, Access application/policy, and identity provider.
A Tunnel with cloudflared connectors able to reach the origin.
Origin application with its own application-level authorization and session handling where required.
flows: The browser resolves app.example.com and connects to Cloudflare over HTTPS.
Access evaluates the application policy and completes identity-provider authentication when needed.
Allowed requests travel through the Tunnel to cloudflared. Configure Protect with Access to validate the application JWT before proxying to the origin.
cloudflared connects to the origin service; the response returns through the tunnel and Cloudflare to the browser.
trustBoundaries: The identity provider establishes identity; the Access policy determines application access. A Tunnel route alone does not authorize a user.
The connector-to-origin network is a separate trust boundary. Use verified origin TLS where the threat model requires it; do not disable certificate validation to hide a configuration fault.
Remove or restrict alternate origin hostnames, public ports, and direct-IP paths that bypass Access. Validate JWTs in the origin when its exposure model requires defense in depth.
routingAndDns: Route the public hostname to the correct tunnel using the documented DNS setup. Keep full-zone and partial-CNAME setup procedures distinct.
Match the intended hostname to the intended origin service and use a non-proxying catch-all for unmatched ingress.
Avoid mixing path-dependent ingress with stronger policy assumptions without testing normalization and matching on the deployed cloudflared version.
identityPolicy: Start with a narrowly scoped group and required identity conditions, not a broad allow-everyone policy.
Set and test application session behavior and revocation expectations. Keep origin authorization for per-resource permissions.
For connector JWT validation, use the correct Access team and application audience. Never trust the mere presence of Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion.
failureModes: Identity-provider or Access authentication failures prevent new sign-ins; cached session behavior depends on the configured policy and token lifetime.
Connector or outbound-network loss makes that path unavailable. Multiple connectors provide redundancy only if each can reach the required origin.
Origin DNS, TLS, or application failures can occur while the tunnel remains connected. Monitor the application path, not just connector status.
Replicas of one tunnel are not a substitute for health-aware application traffic steering. Load Balancing is a separate design and entitlement decision.
tradeoffs: Browser-based access avoids a client installation for this public web scenario, but creates a discoverable public application hostname.
Access and origin sessions introduce separate expiry, recovery, and support concerns.
Removing direct public ingress reduces bypass paths but makes tested connector redundancy and recovery important.
body.diagramText:
Browser --HTTPS--> Cloudflare / Access --Tunnel--> cloudflared --verified origin connection--> Web application
Access <--> Identity provider
Boundary 1: user identity and Access policy. Boundary 2: connector-to-origin reachability and TLS. Tunnel is transport, not an authorization decision.
validation: Confirm an allowed user reaches the app and a user outside the policy cannot.
Confirm anonymous requests cannot reach the protected origin; test direct-IP and alternate-hostname bypass paths.
Test invalid/absent application JWT handling at the configured validation layer.
Stop one connector in an approved test and observe application availability; separately test an origin failure and recovery.
rollback: Keep an owner-approved, authenticated recovery path independent of the application being changed.
Revert the specific route or policy change rather than opening the origin or broadly bypassing Access.
Restore connector/origin health and retest allowed, denied, and bypass cases before restoring normal traffic.

title: Make D1 creation recoverable after a lost response
summary: Commit an item and an actor-scoped idempotency receipt in one D1 batch. Recover the recorded result on a same-key retry without claiming exactly-once delivery or retrying arbitrary writes.

requires: A TypeScript Worker with a generated Env type and a local D1 DB binding.
A trusted authentication layer that supplies the actor, bounded validated input, and a client key reused only for unchanged retries.
excludes: This repository example is not a complete HTTP handler or an authorization system.
It does not atomically coordinate email, external APIs, or a cache purge with a D1 transaction.
dependencies: Keep the database binding local during development; never use remote: true for this rehearsal.
Confirm Workers/D1 quotas, row and index costs, receipt retention, and backup requirements for the intended workload.

prerequisites: Generate Env from a Wrangler configuration with a DB binding; the example uses Env['DB'] rather than a hand-written binding interface.
Authenticate before calling the repository. Bound streamed JSON bytes before buffering, then validate the key and value. Do not accept an actor supplied by the request body.
Use a fixed operation namespace and canonical payload shape. Decide receipt retention before launch.
steps: Apply the two-table schema locally. The unique actor/operation/key tuple is the durable concurrency boundary.
Compute the canonical payload digest and check the receipt using a first-primary session. A completed key with different data is a conflict.
Insert the item and receipt in one batch. A receipt uniqueness failure rolls back the item insert.

If the commit response is lost or a concurrent request wins, read the receipt and return its item ID only when the digest agrees. If no receipt exists, surface the error and let a bounded unchanged retry recover later.

Map the repository conflict to HTTP 409 and successful creation/replay to the documented response. Apply any required cache purge after both initial success and replay; a purge failure does not undo the commit.

artifacts.purpose: A small independent example, not a migration for this catalog. Retain receipts with their items and include both in private recovery backups.
Durable creation only. Call after authentication and bounded validation; the caller owns HTTP errors, bounded retry policy, and any cache invalidation.

artifacts.text: Do not log tokens, request bodies, or raw idempotency keys. Do not delete a receipt to make a conflicting retry succeed. External side effects require an additional design, such as a transactional outbox.

validation: Repeat the same actor/key/value: one item, one receipt, and the same ID.
Reuse the same actor/key with another value: conflict, with no extra item.
Run concurrent unchanged requests and simulate a response lost after commit; both must resolve to one committed item.
Force the receipt insert to fail and confirm the item insert rolls back.
Test streamed multibyte and misleading-length payloads at the HTTP boundary. Test cache-purge failures and replay purge attempts separately.
rollback: Roll back application code without dropping receipts or resetting identity sequences.
Keep the operation namespace and canonical payload stable across the compatibility window.
Restore from a private backup containing both items and receipts when recovery is needed. A public catalog export is not a recovery backup.
